summary.text: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers or other mathematical objects, with entries arranged in rows and columns.
In linear algebra matrices are used as linear maps, and in geometry they describe transformations such as rotations.
Matrices are used in most areas of mathematics and scientific fields, either directly or through geometry and numerical analysis.

items.explain: A square matrix is invertible if and only if it has a nonzero determinant.

paragraphs.heading: A grid of entries
paragraphs.text: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers, or of other mathematical objects, laid out in rows and columns. The items in it are called its entries or elements. Rows are the horizontal lines of entries and columns are the vertical ones. With m rows and n columns, a matrix is called an m × n matrix, and m and n are its dimensions.

paragraphs.heading: Shapes with names
paragraphs.text: Some shapes get their own names. A matrix with a single row is a row vector, and one with a single column is a column vector. A square matrix has as many rows as columns, and square matrices play a major role in matrix theory. There are also infinite matrices, with endlessly many rows or columns, and empty matrices with no rows or no columns, which are handy in computer algebra programs.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: In linear algebra, matrices act as linear maps. In geometry they describe transformations such as rotations, and changes of coordinates too. In numerical analysis, many problems are solved by turning them into matrix calculations, often with enormous matrices. Through these routes, matrices reach most areas of mathematics and the sciences.

paragraphs.heading: How they are written
paragraphs.text: Matrices are usually named with capital letters such as A, while a lowercase letter with two subscripts, such as a₁₁, names one entry. Many authors also print matrices in bold to set them apart from other objects. Sometimes the entries come from a formula, a_(i,j) = f(i, j). Some programming languages count rows and columns from zero instead of from one.

paragraphs.heading: Doing arithmetic
paragraphs.text: Several basic operations work on matrices. Some, such as transposition, do not depend on what kind of entries the matrix holds. Others, including addition, scalar multiplication and matrix multiplication, act on the entries, so the entries must be numbers or belong to a field or a ring. Addition behaves like ordinary addition, so A + B = B + A. Multiplication obeys (AB)C = A(BC) whenever the sizes allow the products.

paragraphs.heading: Order matters
paragraphs.text: Matrix multiplication has a twist. The product AB can exist while BA does not, for example when A is m × n, B is n × k, and m ≠ k. Even when both products exist, they need not be equal: 𝐀𝐁 ≠ 𝐁𝐀.

paragraphs.heading: The determinant
paragraphs.text: Every square matrix has a number called its determinant, which is central to studying it. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is not zero. Its eigenvalues are the roots of det (λI − A), which is called its characteristic polynomial.

paragraphs.heading: A field of its own
paragraphs.text: Matrix theory is the part of mathematics devoted to matrices. It began as a branch of linear algebra but soon grew to take in topics linked to graph theory, algebra, combinatorics and statistics.
